opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Before that work, most 6D object pose estimation in robotics was instance-level. You'd have an exact CAD model of a specific object, say one particular mug or drill, and the system would learn to find that exact object and estimate its rotation and translation. That works well in a controlled factory setting, but it doesn't scale to the real world. In a home there are thousands of mugs, bowls, bottles and laptops, and you'll never have a precise CAD model for each one.

So the question I kept asking was this: humans don't need a 3D model of a specific mug to know how to grab it. We understand "mugness." We know where the handle usually is, which way is up, roughly how big it is. Can a robot have that kind of category-level understanding?

That's what led to the idea of the Normalized Object Coordinate Space, NOCS. The key insight was to define a shared, canonical coordinate frame for all objects in a category. All mugs are aligned to the same orientation and normalized to the same scale. Then, for a novel instance the network has never seen, it predicts for each pixel where that point would sit in the canonical space. Matching those predictions against depth observations recovers the full 6D pose and the object's size, even for an unseen instance.

I saw it as a meaningful extension for a few reasons. First, it moves pose estimation from recognition toward generalization, which is what robots actually need outside the lab. Second, it connects vision with action. Pose isn't just a perception output; it's the interface for manipulation. Once you know an object's canonical frame, you can transfer grasps or skills defined on that frame to new instances. Third, it surfaced a broader research theme I've continued to pursue: how to learn representations that are structured and geometric enough to support reasoning and interaction, yet general enough to handle the diversity of the real world.

Looking back, it was an early step toward what we now talk about as generalizable embodied intelligence. Robots can't succeed by memorizing specific objects; they need abstractions at the level of categories, parts and affordances. Category-level pose was one of the first concrete, solvable versions of that bigger problem.

r001.rationale: The response describes pose as rotation and translation, but does not compare it with discrete attributes such as open or closed.

r002.rationale: It identifies the need for an exact CAD model of a specific object as a limitation, but does not say that instance-level estimation requires a separate coordinate frame for each instance.

r003.rationale: It says people understand category-level properties such as a mug’s handle and orientation, but does not state that people describe pose relative to an imagined canonical orientation shared by the category.

r004.rationale: It explains that a shared canonical coordinate space lets the network estimate pose and size for a novel, unseen instance without a coordinate frame defined specifically for that instance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. To answer that, I have to go back a bit. When I was doing my PhD at Stanford with Leonidas Guibas, most of the work on object pose estimation was instance-level. You have a specific object, you have its exact CAD model, and you want to know where it is and how it's oriented in the scene. That works beautifully in a controlled setting. But it fundamentally doesn't scale. In the real world, a robot walks into a kitchen and sees a mug it has never seen before. There is no CAD model for that mug. So the instance-level formulation, as elegant as it is, basically breaks on contact with reality.

What struck me was that humans don't work that way at all. You don't need to have seen this particular mug to know how to pick it up by the handle. You know what mugs are. You have a notion of the category, and that notion carries a kind of canonical structure: the handle is here, the opening is on top, the body is roughly cylindrical. So the question we asked was: can we give a vision system that same ability? Can it estimate the 6D pose and the size of an object given only that it belongs to a known category?

Technically, the hard part was that pose is not even well-defined across instances. Two chairs have different geometry, so what does it mean for them to share a rotation? Our answer in the NOCS work was to define a normalized canonical space per category, so every instance gets mapped into the same unit cube with a consistent orientation. Once you have that shared coordinate frame, the problem becomes tractable, and you can predict dense correspondences from an image into that space and solve for pose and scale.

I saw it as a meaningful extension because it shifted the question from "where is this known thing" to "where is this kind of thing," and that second question is the one robots actually need answered. It also opened a lot of doors afterward, toward articulated objects, toward manipulation, toward thinking about what representations generalize. So for me it was less about a single benchmark and more about moving the field one step closer to open-world perception.

r002.rationale: It says instance-level estimation relies on an exact CAD model, but does not identify defining a coordinate frame separately for each instance as a limitation.

r003.rationale: It describes category-level canonical structure, but does not say humans describe pose relative to an imagined canonical orientation shared by the category.

r004.rationale: It says the system can estimate pose for an unseen instance based on category membership and describes mapping instances to a shared category-level canonical frame.

astra-6.text:
I saw it as a way to move robot perception beyond recognizing objects it had already seen. In instance-level pose estimation, you typically assume you have an exact model of the object. But a robot working in an everyday environment will encounter new cups, bowls, or bottles, with different shapes and sizes. It still needs to understand where they are and how they’re oriented to interact with them.

Category-level pose estimation asks whether we can use what those objects share to estimate the pose of an unfamiliar instance. The interesting challenge is that you need to generalize across shape variation while preserving the geometric precision that manipulation requires. That made it a meaningful extension for me: connecting recognition at the category level with the spatial understanding a robot needs to act.

r001.rationale: The response discusses estimating an object's position and orientation, but does not compare 6D pose with discrete attributes such as open or closed.

r002.rationale: It says instance-level estimation typically assumes an exact object model, but does not identify defining a separate coordinate frame for each instance as a limitation.

r003.rationale: It discusses shared category features, but does not describe humans imagining a canonical orientation shared by the category.

r004.rationale: It says category-level estimation can handle an unfamiliar instance, but does not state that this avoids defining a coordinate frame specifically for that instance.

sol-6.1.text:
What made it meaningful to me was the gap between recognizing an object and knowing how to interact with it. A robot might recognize a mug, but to pick it up, it also needs to understand its position, orientation, and size.

With instance-level pose estimation, you typically assume you have an exact 3D model of the object. That’s useful in a controlled setting, but it becomes limiting when a robot encounters objects it hasn’t seen before. Category-level pose estimation asks whether we can transfer what we know about a category to a new instance, even though its shape and proportions are different.

So it was a natural extension toward more general robot perception: giving the robot a useful geometric understanding of unfamiliar objects without requiring a model of every individual one.

r002.rationale: It identifies reliance on an exact 3D model as a limitation, but does not mention defining a separate coordinate frame for each instance.

r003.rationale: It does not describe humans using an imagined canonical orientation shared by a category.

r004.rationale: It says category knowledge can transfer to an unseen instance without a model of every individual, but does not state that this avoids defining an instance-specific coordinate frame.
